segments.text: Welcome back. Today we look at loops in
Python, starting with the for loop. A for loop
repeats a block of code once
for every item in a sequence. The sequence
can be a list, a string, or a range of
numbers. Let us write one together.
We type for, then a variable name, then in,
then the sequence, and a colon
at the end. Everything indented under
that line is the body of
the loop. Python runs the body once
per item, and each time the variable holds the next
item. So if the list holds
three numbers, the body runs three
times. A very common pattern is the accumulator.
We set a variable called total to
zero before the loop. Inside the loop we add each
item to total. When the loop finishes, total holds the
sum of the whole list. Notice
that the print call sits outside the loop,
so it runs only once, at the end. If you
indent it by mistake, it prints after every item instead.
That is one of the most common bugs students make
with loops. Now let us talk about the range
function. Range gives you a sequence of whole
numbers without writing a list by hand. Range of five
gives zero, one, two, three and four. It
stops before five, which surprises many people
the first time. You can also give
range a start and a stop, and even a step.
Range of two to ten with a step of two
gives the even numbers from two to eight.
Next, the while loop. A while loop keeps
running as long as its condition
is true. Before every pass, Python checks
the condition again. If the condition never
becomes false, the loop runs forever. That is called
an infinite loop, and you stop
it with control C. So inside a while
loop, something must change that eventually makes the condition false.
Usually that means updating a counter at the end of
the body. Finally, the break statement
leaves a loop early, and continue skips to
the next pass. Use them sparingly,
because they make a loop harder to read.
That is all for today, see you next
time.
